newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Opposition to Sierra Leone coup persists.
newsitem.headline: Opposition to Sierra Leone coup persists.

text.p: Public opposition to a weekend coup in Sierra Leone showed no sign of abating on Wednesday, although rebels of the Revolutionary United Front rallied to the new military leaders.
Embassies, aid organisations and United Nations offices prepared to evacuate non-essential staff, and a Lebanese plane flew to Freetown to evacuate about 150 people from the airport.
Civil and professional groups and trade unions condemned the coup, and shops and offices remained closed despite an appeal by the coup leaders for people to return to work.

"We advise all our workers to stay home in the current situation because of the insecurity in the country, especially with the release of hardened criminals from the Pademba Road prison," the Sierra Leone Labour Congress said.

Freetown's new military leader, Major Johnny Paul Koromah, was among those freed from the jail on Sunday morning. He had been held there on treason charges over an alleged coup attempt last September.
Koromah tried to reassure Sierra Leoneans at his first news conference that Nigerian troop reinforcements had come to evacuate their nationals, not to intervene.
But a senior military source said Koromah's Armed Forces Revolutionary Council was under strong pressure to stand aside.
Koromah said there was no cause for alarm. "ECOMOG will not interfere in our internal matters," he said, referring to the Nigerian-led regional force in Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Nigeria has made no public statement on Sunday's coup but officials said it was trying to negotiate a peaceful restoration of civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

A Middle East Airlines plane took off from Ghana for Freetown's Lungi airport to fly out 150 Lebanese nationals. United Nations officials and diplomats met Koromah to discuss an evacuation of a U.N.-chartered boat which arrived on Tuesday.

U.S. State Department spokesman John Dinger said the U.S. Navy helicopter ship Kearsarge was expected to arrive off Sierra Leone's coast late on Wednesday or early Thursday to stand by in case an evacuation was ordered.
Rebel leader Foday Sankoh, in a broadcast on Sierra Leone radio, said his Revolutionary United Front (RUF) rebels and the army now had common cause and he wanted to come home and join the government.
"All RUF field commanders and troops should stand by for any reinforcement needed by Major Koromah to defend our sovereignty," said Sankoh, who is currently held at a hotel in the Nigerian capital.

"I am ready to go to Sierra Leone at any time, I have been longing to go to Sierra Leone these past two, three months. I am here against my democratic rights," he said, appealing to Nigeria's government to let him leave.
"Today and from now on, the RUF and the armed forces of Sierra Leone are one."
Members of a civilian militia whose dissolution was ordered by coup leaders on Sunday said they were ready to march on Freetown to restore Kabbah if necessary.
"We are awaiting word from President Kabbah and we will be in Freetown to help restore order and democracy," said Kamajor commander Eddie Massalay at the Liberian border.
A peace accord signed by Sankoh and Kabbah has failed to hold, and Sankoh is reported to be disillusioned with its terms.
Koromah has banned political activity and suspended the constitution.
His council banned a demonstration called by civilian opponents of the coup for Wednesday to demand the return of Kabbah, whose government was elected in March 1996 after four years of military rule.
At his news conference he apologised for the widespread looting. Asked about the fire at the central bank he described it as "a bad start for my government economically".

Nigeria landed hundreds of troops in Freetown on Tuesday and Wednesday to reinforce the 900 already stationed in the country, after Kabbah asked West African countries for help to restore his elected government.
